source_groups.label: Printed Chapter C header and explicit rejection of transits/profections as rectification
claims: CHAP C The Rectification by Accidents and Speculum
The author begins a distinct numbered nativity-rectification chapter based on accidents and an astrological speculum.
Printed Chapter C is editorial/sequential CI, not the earlier Animodar chapter.

figure of Profections directing ascendant and Mid-heaven

Do not conflate profection with the method Lilly favors.
could never finde any verity or probability
Lilly explicitly reports finding no reliability in either transit- or profection-based correction in his practice.
Unquantified author opinion, not a controlled demonstration of zero predictive performance.
He refers readers interested in those discarded methods to Origanus.
The referenced passage has not been reaudited.
He cites John Schoner's attempt to rectify his own birth chart using profections.
One historical self-case, not a verified independent outcome.
He also cites Pezelius for earlier practical descriptions.
The precise source identity and text remain unchecked.
He recommends using significant personal events that have already occurred to rectify a natal chart.
Retrospective curve fitting: those same events cannot establish out-of-sample predictive accuracy.
collect so many as he can procure and eminent ones
He asks for as many significant life events as can be obtained.
An open event-selection set creates flexibility; denominator is not frozen.
certaine time ... yeer and moneth day
Ideally the events have known year, month, and day.
Precise date is preferred but not required.
moneth and yeer will well serve
Lilly permits using only month and year when no exact day is available.
accept of the yeer without moneth
If needed he allows a year-only event date.
Very broad timing window; not equivalent to a day-specific hit.
For bodily conditions he prioritizes illnesses, misfortunes, and physical calamities.
Retrospective outcomes; not current clinical diagnoses.
The Ascendant and its progression supply the significator for bodily accidents.
The progressed degree is chosen from an estimated natal chart.
A planet encountered by conjunction or aspect supplies a promissor associated with the adverse event.
The source includes interpretive classification of promissors.
he shewes greatness and quality of accident
The selected promissor is said to indicate severity and kind of event.

source_groups.label: Original 12-sign full-circle speculum schema and manually placed aspect glyphs
claims: An Astrological Speculum of our Nativity
A large twelve-column chart shows natal planetary aspects, terms and future directed contact positions.
Primary numeric/graphical source witness; all glyph coordinates are retained in the original JPEG.
The zodiac signs form successive 30° columns across the full 360° ecliptic.
The 0–30 degree row indexing is continuous through signs.
The left-most table column includes degree and minutes of sign.
Some rows have minute offsets, not uniform exact degrees.
Symbols of Planets Terms and Aspects
The grid includes term ruler glyphs and traditional aspect positions.
These hand-entered markups are not an independently validated aspect database.
The worksheet includes antiscia and contra-antiscia signs such as 'An.' and 'CA'.
Reflection formulas/glyphs need independent diplomatic and mathematical checking.
A 'M.C.' label near 14°39 marks the Midheaven in the natal speculum.
The sign and exact row should not be invented from a low-resolution chart.

The chart marks the natal ascendant near 6°37 of its sign.
Estimated chart; later author intentionally adjusts it.
manual speculum glyphs thousands of potential intersections
The original sheet encodes many candidate contacts over multiple signs, rows and aspect types.
One-image-page documentary record cannot be counted as complete machine-readable extraction of individual placements.
